clinicalPearls: Diabetic kidney disease is a leading cause of end-stage renal failure and usually develops after years of diabetes
The earliest clinical marker is moderately increased albuminuria (microalbuminuria), which can progress to overt proteinuria and declining filtration
Screening with an annual urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and estimated GFR allows early detection and intervention
Coexistent diabetic retinopathy supports a diabetic aetiology, and its absence in type 1 diabetes should prompt consideration of an alternative renal diagnosis
Tight control of both blood glucose and blood pressure slows progression, and blockade of the renin-angiotensin system is renoprotective in albuminuric patients
SGLT2 inhibitors reduce progression of diabetic kidney disease and cardiovascular risk and have become central to management
Features such as active urinary sediment, rapid GFR loss, or heavy proteinuria without retinopathy warrant evaluation for a non-diabetic renal disease
reference.pathophysiology: Sustained hyperglycaemia and glomerular hypertension drive haemodynamic and metabolic injury to the kidney. Early glomerular hyperfiltration, mesangial expansion, glomerular basement membrane thickening, and podocyte injury progress to nodular and diffuse glomerulosclerosis, the nodular lesions being the classic Kimmelstiel-Wilson change. Advanced glycation end-products, oxidative stress, and activation of the renin-angiotensin system promote albuminuria, tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and progressive loss of filtration.
additionalDifferentials: Glomerulonephritis or other primary glomerular disease
Membranous nephropathy or minimal change disease presenting with nephrotic-range proteinuria
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis to assess for haematuria or active sediment suggesting an alternative cause
Dilated retinal examination to look for concurrent retinopathy
Renal ultrasound and, in atypical presentations, consideration of renal biopsy
redFlags: Rapidly declining GFR out of proportion to expected diabetic course
Active urinary sediment, red cell casts, or nephrotic syndrome without retinopathy
Uncontrolled hypertension with worsening renal function
Signs of advanced uraemia or fluid overload requiring renal replacement planning
reference.prognosis: Without intervention diabetic nephropathy progresses to end-stage renal disease and carries a high cardiovascular mortality, but early detection and aggressive control of glucose and blood pressure, renin-angiotensin blockade, and SGLT2 inhibition can substantially slow progression.
pitfalls: Assuming all renal impairment in a diabetic patient is diabetic nephropathy and missing a treatable alternative
Failing to screen for albuminuria and losing the window for early renoprotective therapy
Under-using renin-angiotensin blockade and SGLT2 inhibitors in eligible patients
Neglecting cardiovascular risk, which is the dominant cause of death in these patients
management: Blockade the renin-angiotensin system with an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin-receptor blocker, which is renoprotective in albuminuric patients
Use an SGLT2 inhibitor to slow progression of kidney disease and reduce cardiovascular risk
Achieve tight control of both blood glucose and blood pressure to slow the decline in filtration
Consider a non-steroidal mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist to reduce residual albuminuria in appropriate patients
Screen and monitor with annual urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and estimated GFR, and check potassium on renin-angiotensin-blocking therapy
Manage cardiovascular risk with lipid-lowering therapy and lifestyle measures
Refer to nephrology when the picture is atypical or disease advances, and prepare for dialysis or transplantation in end-stage disease
